newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: US tackles Kazakh ruler over widespread corruption.
newsitem.headline: US tackles Kazakh ruler over widespread corruption.

text.p: With a tough winter ahead for Kazakhstan, President Nursultan Nazarbayev on Wednesday faced awkward questions from a senior American official on corruption in the former Soviet republic.
U.S. Ambassador-at-Large James Collins, special advisor on the former Soviet republics, was in the Kazakh capital Almaty for bilateral talks with Nazarbayev and other politicians.
A senior western diplomat in Almaty told Reuters: "He's talked about the need to deal with crime and corruption. It's a real drag and impediment on western interests."
Ambassador Richard Morningside, travelling with Collins, told a news conference: "It's necessary to establish a rule of law - it's a factor in bringing investment to Kazakhstan."

The oil-rich Central Asian nation, five times the size of France, is sitting on billions of dollars worth of oil, gas and metals. Around $800 million of American investment has flowed into Kazakhstan this year.
But foreign investors are alarmed at what they describe as endemic corruption in the republic.
The head of a foreign mining company on the hunt for deals in the Central Asia region said of Kazakhstan: "The corruption is unbelievable -- we just had to quit looking there."
Nazarbayev desperately needs foreign investment to shore up the Kazakh economy and counter impatience among the 16.9 million population over unpaid salaries and pensions.
Nazarbayev, Kazakhstan's former Communist Party leader, speaks regularly about his determination to crackdown on crime.
As if on cue, he published a decree in the official press on Wednesday ordering senior officials to declare their income and property.

But it will cheer few of the population. After the first snows had fallen on Almaty last week, many residents had to boil water on fires in the streets after supplies of gas from neighbouring Uzbekistan were shut off.
One western aid worker based in Almaty, who declined to be named, said his agency was considering an appeal to combat malnutrition in Kazakhstan's hard-hit regions.

"We don't need lectures in macro-economics and how they're building a market," said Pyotr Svoik, a leading member of Azamat, a loose coalition of opposition parties and trade unions. "We need our salaries, gas, electricity, pensions."
Svoik was speaking last week at an Azamat meeting in a battered trade union building to complain to journalists that official permission for a demonstration had been denied.
Trade union leader Galina Sevrukova said: "Western investors should know they finance a totalitarian system, there is no democracy here."

Nazarbayev, up for re-election in 2000, has substantial executive powers but tolerates political dissent. The strongmen leaders in neighbouring Uzbekistan and Turkemenistan would never have allowed such an opposition news conference to take place.
Kazakh security forces stood by and watched on Sunday as Svoik and Sevrukova went ahead with their protest -- only 400 people turned up.
But Nazarbayev is under pressure both at home and abroad to establish more open government.
Private broadcasters lashed out at the sudden removal of frequencies from four private radio stations -- the government denied any political motive, citing "technical" reasons.
